Trying to Conceive

Laparoscopy and dye testing: checking whether the fallopian tubes are open

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A laparoscopy and dye test, also called chromopertubation, examines the pelvis and checks whether fluid can pass through the fallopian tubes. It can help plan fertility care, but an open tube does not guarantee pregnancy and an apparent blockage needs careful interpretation. Because it involves an operation and usually general anaesthesia, it is not the first test for everyone.

What the test checks

The fallopian tubes connect the area near the ovaries to the uterus. For conception without IVF, sperm and an egg usually meet in a tube. Scarring, infection or other damage can interfere with passage or the movement of an embryo towards the uterus.

During dye testing, the clinician puts a small tube through the cervix and introduces coloured fluid into the uterus. A camera used during laparoscopy lets the surgeon look for fluid emerging from each fallopian tube. The test checks passage at that time; it does not measure every aspect of tubal function.

Why laparoscopy may be offered

Fertility assessment usually starts with less invasive investigations and considers ovulation, the uterus and tubes, and semen where relevant. HSG or an appropriate contrast ultrasound test may assess tubal passage without abdominal surgery. Routine laparoscopy is not recommended for every person having difficulty conceiving.

Laparoscopy with dye may be useful when pelvic disease is suspected, for example after pelvic inflammatory disease or an ectopic pregnancy, or when endometriosis or adhesions need assessment. If surgery is already indicated, dye testing may answer an additional question. Ask what decision the result would change in your particular situation.

What happens during the operation

The team confirms the agreed procedure and checks pregnancy and anaesthetic safety. Under general anaesthesia, the surgeon usually makes small abdominal incisions, introduces gas to create working space and uses a camera to examine the pelvis. The dye is delivered through the cervix, not injected into an ovary.

The surgeon observes whether dye passes from one or both tubes and looks for visible abnormalities around the tubes, ovaries and uterus. The time required depends on the findings and any separately agreed treatment. A diagnostic operation and a more extensive therapeutic operation have different recovery needs.

Understanding spill and apparent blockage

Spill from a tube supports that it was open during the test. It does not prove that its delicate lining and transport function are normal, or rule out other causes of infertility. Neither a normal dye test nor a normal-looking pelvis guarantees that pregnancy will follow.

No visible spill may indicate obstruction, but the test has limitations. The team considers technical factors, the site of the apparent blockage and the rest of the investigation before making a lasting treatment decision. Further assessment, sometimes including selective tubal catheter testing, may be appropriate for suspected blockage near the uterus.

If one or both tubes are affected

The implications depend on whether blockage is confirmed, where it lies and how much damage is present. With one functioning tube, conception without IVF may still be possible. Confirmed complete blockage of both tubes prevents the usual tubal route for sperm and egg to meet, but it does not mean that all pregnancy options are closed.

IVF can bypass the tubes. The choice between further assessment, selected tubal surgery and IVF also depends on age, ovarian reserve, semen findings, other conditions, preferences and available services. Neither surgery nor IVF promises a baby. Tubal damage and some tubal operations increase ectopic-pregnancy risk; ask about early pregnancy follow-up.

Testing is different from treatment

Dye passing through the tubes is not a promise that blockage has been cured. In selected circumstances, a surgeon may treat adhesions or endometriosis, attempt tubal repair or recommend removing or blocking a severely damaged fluid-filled tube before IVF. These are separate treatment decisions with their own benefits and risks.

Discuss possible additional procedures before the operation, including whether you agree to repair or removal and what should happen if an unexpected finding appears. Removal is not an automatic consequence of a dye result. Repair can fail or a tube can close again, and surgery can itself lead to adhesions. Ask about alternatives, including postponing treatment for a fuller discussion when safe.

Risks to discuss beforehand

Laparoscopy can cause bleeding, infection, damage to bowel, bladder, blood vessels, nerves or other structures, a hernia or new adhesions. Occasionally a larger incision or another operation is needed. Passing instruments through the cervix can rarely injure the uterus. Individual risks depend on health, previous operations and the planned procedure.

Anaesthesia and medicines can cause nausea, sore throat or other side effects; serious reactions and blood clots are possible. Tell the team about previous reactions to anaesthesia, medicines or contrast agents. A prior abdominal operation or an allergy history is a reason for individual planning, not automatically a permanent ban on every test.

Preparing for a safe procedure

Follow the hospital’s own instructions about pregnancy avoidance or testing, cycle timing, infection checks, fasting and medicines. Tell the team if pregnancy is possible, you develop an illness or infection, or your medicines have changed. Do not stop prescribed medicines or start antibiotics on your own.

Bring an accurate medicine and allergy list, including supplements, and describe previous surgical or anaesthetic problems. Arrange transport home and an adult to stay with you as advised after general anaesthesia. Discuss childcare, work and access needs beforehand, and ask for a written plan and a contact number for problems after discharge.

Recovery and everyday activities

Mild abdominal discomfort, bloating, tiredness, light vaginal bleeding or shoulder discomfort from the gas can occur after laparoscopy. Symptoms should follow the recovery pattern explained by your team. New severe or worsening pain, or shoulder pain with pelvic pain, must not simply be labelled trapped gas.

Use the pain relief and wound-care plan you were given, move gently and use clot-prevention measures if prescribed. Driving, work, lifting, bathing, sex and trying to conceive depend on the anaesthetic, procedure and recovery: follow your own discharge instructions. Do not drive, drink alcohol, operate machinery or care for children alone during the restriction period after general anaesthesia.

HSG: an X-ray alternative

A hysterosalpingogram, or HSG, uses contrast placed through the cervix and X-ray images to assess the uterine cavity and tubal passage. It is usually an outpatient test without abdominal incisions or general anaesthesia. It does not give the same direct view of the outside of pelvic organs as laparoscopy.

Cramping, infection and a reaction to the contrast are possible, and the test uses a small radiation dose. Pregnancy must be excluded and previous contrast reactions reported. Apparent blockage, particularly near the uterus, can need confirmation. Appointment length and preparation vary; do not assume every alternative takes less than ten minutes.

HyCoSy: a contrast ultrasound alternative

Hysterosalpingo contrast sonography, or HyCoSy, follows ultrasound-visible contrast introduced through the cervix, usually with a vaginal ultrasound scan. It avoids X-ray radiation and abdominal surgery. Suitability depends on the clinical question, available expertise and the ability to obtain clear images.

Cramping, an incomplete test and uncommon complications such as infection or a contrast reaction can occur. Pregnancy and infection checks follow the clinic’s protocol. Ordinary saline sonohysterography mainly evaluates the uterine cavity: seeing fluid in the pelvis alone does not show that each tube is open. Ask exactly which ultrasound test is proposed.

Making a plan from the results

Ask for an explanation of each tube’s findings, any other pelvic abnormality, the limits of the test and whether treatment was performed. Find out how to obtain the operative report and when to review it alongside the rest of the fertility assessment. A result described as normal does not make continuing difficulties or symptoms unimportant.

If repair, tube removal or IVF is proposed, discuss the reason, realistic benefits, recovery, ectopic risk and alternatives. Comparisons of treatment success depend on age and other factors and may use different measures. You can ask for time, an interpreter, fertility counselling or another opinion before a non-emergency decision.

When to seek urgent or emergency help

After the procedure, seek urgent medical advice for fever or feeling hot, cold or shivery, severe or persistent vomiting, worsening abdominal pain or swelling, wound redness, pain, swelling, bleeding or pus, unusual vaginal or rectal bleeding or discharge, a painful swollen leg, coughing blood or breathlessness. Follow the discharge team’s emergency instructions; do not wait for a routine follow-up appointment.

Call emergency services for chest pain, a very fast heartbeat or severe breathing difficulty. Pelvic pain that is severe, worsening or hurts with movement or touch also needs emergency assessment, as does pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy vaginal bleeding or sudden confusion. These are alternatives, not a checklist requiring every sign. Do not drive yourself. If pregnancy is possible, pelvic pain or unusual bleeding needs prompt assessment even without a positive test.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Choose a test according to the clinical question and likely effect on treatment.

Interpret each tube’s result alongside the whole fertility assessment.

Agree on consent, discharge instructions and a follow-up plan before surgery.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize appointment questions, medicines and the results discussion. It cannot interpret a surgical finding, diagnose a complication or monitor an emergency; recording information must not delay care.

When to seek help

Call emergency services for chest pain, a very fast heartbeat or severe breathing difficulty. Severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain with movement or touch, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or sudden confusion also needs emergency assessment. Do not wait for every sign or drive yourself. Other postoperative warning signs in this guide need urgent medical advice. Possible pregnancy with pelvic pain or unusual bleeding needs prompt assessment even without a positive test.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Dye testing shows passage through the tubes at one point in time; it does not guarantee normal function or pregnancy.
  • Laparoscopy is selected for a clinical reason; HSG or HyCoSy may answer the question with less invasive testing.
  • Repair, removal and IVF are separate decisions requiring individual counselling and consent.
  • Follow your own preparation and recovery plan, including anaesthetic restrictions and the results appointment.
  • Do not dismiss severe pain, breathing problems, faintness or other warning signs as normal postoperative gas.

Frequently asked questions

What is chromopertubation?

It is a dye test of tubal passage performed during laparoscopy. Fluid is introduced through the cervix into the uterus, and the surgeon looks for it leaving each tube. The camera also permits examination of the pelvis.

Why not offer it to everyone with infertility?

It requires surgery and usually general anaesthesia. Less invasive tests may answer the tubal question, while laparoscopy is selected when suspected pelvic disease or another indication makes its additional information useful.

Does dye spill mean I will become pregnant?

No. It supports that the tube was open during the test, but does not establish normal transport function or exclude ovulatory, semen or other fertility factors.

Can both blocked tubes be repaired?

Sometimes selected damage can be treated, but repair is not suitable or successful in every case and re-blockage can occur. Confirm the finding and discuss the site and severity, ectopic risk and alternatives such as IVF.

Does bilateral blockage mean pregnancy is impossible?

Confirmed complete blockage of both tubes prevents the usual tubal route, but IVF can bypass the tubes. The appropriate options and chances depend on the whole fertility assessment, not the dye result alone.

Will a damaged tube be removed automatically?

No. Planned repair or removal should be discussed and consented to separately, including what to do if unexpected findings appear. Ask why removal is proposed and how it affects fertility options.

Is an ultrasound test the same as laparoscopy and dye?

No. HyCoSy follows contrast using ultrasound without abdominal surgery; HSG uses X-rays. Ordinary saline ultrasound of the uterine cavity is not automatically a test showing that both tubes are open.

Which symptoms must not wait after the operation?

Emergency signs include chest pain, a very fast heartbeat, severe breathing difficulty, severe or worsening pelvic pain or pain with movement or touch, and pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or sudden confusion. Seek urgent advice for the other postoperative warning signs listed above. Do not wait for several signs or drive yourself.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
